title: How to avoid bicep tears
summary: Explains where biceps tears happen and how to prevent them. Avoid heavy supinated pulls from the floor (mixed-grip deadlifts, underhand rows, supinated shrugs), keep a slight bend at the bottom of every curl instead of locking out, and be careful on preacher curls and high rows. He credits these rules for 10 years of heavy curling without injury.

claims.claim: Biceps tears are serious; depending on the location, some can be surgically reattached and some cannot, which would ruin a bodybuilder's biceps peak.
Never pull heavy from the floor or blocks with a supinated grip, whether a mixed-grip deadlift or, worse, an underhand bent-over row; the extra lat engagement isn't worth it.
Even if you're careful with range of motion, the one day you lose focus and overextend the biceps can snap, and then it must be surgically reattached.
The dangerous supinated lifts are the heavy ones where the biceps is a secondary mover; the biceps shouldn't serve as a stabilizer or as a way to lift more with the prime mover.
Chin-ups are the exception: the angle and the fact that the back is what fully extends make them safe, especially bodyweight chin-ups.
Vertical pulls are generally safe with a supinated grip; horizontal rows, especially standing ones, are where supinated grips are risky (Meadows rows may be tolerated supinated by some).
Never do mixed-grip or supinated shrugs.
Heavy curls can hurt the biceps; protect it by keeping a slight flex at the bottom instead of fully extending, because the last inch mostly stretches the tendon rather than the muscle.
Drop that last 'safety inch' of range on every biceps movement: you'll get more reps and volume and stay safe longer; ignore people calling it half-repping.
Be extra careful on preacher curls because the angle changes; don't give full elbow extension at the bottom, keep the arm slightly flexed and tense.
The heavier the curls, the more dangerous for the biceps.
He has done heavy cheat curls nearly every week for 10 years (120 lbs EZ-bar curls, 80 lbs dumbbell preacher curls) and never had tendinitis, a biceps injury or a tear, thanks to these rules.
On gymnastic rings, holding above the rings with straight arms is safe (isometric); when hanging below and pulling, don't fully extend the arms.
Supinated rows and mixed-grip deadlifts tend to tear the biceps at the forearm (distal) attachment.
High rows can cause 'lawnmower' tears, like older people starting a lawnmower; don't do high rows supinated.
Atlas stones and arm wrestling cause biceps tears at other locations, so strongmen and arm wrestlers should watch out; bodybuilders usually tear at the distal end.

exercises.why: avoid: puts the biceps in a weak position under heavy load

exercises.name: Supinated barbell row
exercises.why: avoid: more lats isn't worth the tear risk

exercises.name: Chin-up
exercises.why: safe supinated pull because the back extends fully, not the biceps

exercises.name: EZ-bar curl
cues: keep a slight flex at the bottom
skip the last inch of extension
exercises.why: last inch only stretches the tendon

exercises.name: Preacher curl
cues: no full elbow extension at the bottom
keep arm slightly flexed and tense
exercises.why: angle increases stress on the tendon
